---
title: "12. Objections and limits"
aliases:
  - /objections.html
---

A model that claims to resolve a long-standing puzzle should expect
pushback, and the same five objections come up wherever the model is
presented. The first half of this chapter states each objection in the
reader's voice and answers it, with links to the chapters that hold the
evidence.

The second half covers where the model misses, which a paper abstract
never tells you. Every model is wrong somewhere, and you can only use a
model safely if you know where it is wrong. If you take one chapter of
the course into a meeting where someone proposes to act on the model's
numbers, take chapter 12.

## "Epstein-Zin preferences are exotic."

They are the minimal structure that separates risk aversion from the
elasticity of intertemporal substitution.
[Chapter 4](04-epstein-zin-preferences.qmd) builds them from that
requirement. Power utility forces the two attitudes to be equal, and
log utility prices the value premium at exactly zero. The separation is
all the model needs, and without the separation long-run news has no
price. The course is an existence proof, not a truth claim. It shows
one internally consistent economy in which the value premium is
compensation for measured risk.

## "Consumption-based pricing failed."

The famous failure was power utility pricing short-run consumption
betas, the rejection documented by
[Hansen and Jagannathan (1991)](../reference/references.qmd). Here the
characteristic is different. Cash flows load on the persistent
component of consumption, and returns never enter the estimation.
[Chapter 8](08-calibrating-cash-flows.qmd) shows the evidence that the
loadings are present in the dividend data. The returns the loadings
predict are checked afterward, in
[Chapter 9](09-the-market-test.qmd) and
[Chapter 10](10-value-premium-resolved.qmd).

## "Firms aren't consumption claims."

They do not need to be. Any dividend process can be projected onto the
consumption moving average, and the projection is the entire estimation
step. The model prices the claim's loading, and it never identifies the
firm with aggregate consumption.
[Chapter 11](11-price-your-own-claim.qmd) walks through the steps for a
claim you bring yourself.

## "We already calibrate a discount rate."

A calibrated level is not a cross-section. A single discount rate, even
a carefully chosen one, assigns the same price of risk to every claim
and therefore cannot say why value should out-earn growth by any amount
other than zero. The model here supplies the dispersion across claims
from measured cash-flow exposures.
[Chapter 1](01-two-free-numbers.qmd) demonstrates that a DCF has two
free numbers and no discipline on either.

## "This is too academic to implement."

Every number in this course is printed at build time by the code cell
above it, from committed data and a published package. Installation to
first valuation is ten seconds, measured on a clean environment. Start
at [Installation](../reference/installation.qmd), or download any
chapter as a notebook and run it.

## Where the model misses

The chapters so far showed the model hitting its targets: the measured
leverages, the market's time series, and the 5.38 percent simulated
value premium of [Chapter 10](10-value-premium-resolved.qmd) against
5.3 in the paper's print. The rest of the chapter lists the places
where the model misses, and what each miss means for how far to trust
the results.

**Return correlations are too low.** Table IX reports a model
value-growth return correlation of 0.44 against 0.75 in the data. The
model separates the two claims by their cash-flow loadings, and the
separation carries over to returns more strongly than in the data,
where common discount-rate variation the model understates moves the
two legs together. Anything that depends on comovement will be
misstated even where the mean premium is right, e.g., hedge ratios
between the legs, the volatility of a long-short portfolio, and
tracking error.

**Value's dividend growth is too persistent.** Table IV shows the
simulated first-order autocorrelation of value's annual dividend growth
at 0.29 against 0.06 in the data. The calibrated cash-flow process
gives value dividends more year-to-year momentum than they display.
The miss is the cost of loading value's dividends heavily on a
persistent state variable. The loading that produces the premium also
produces autocorrelation the data does not fully confirm.

**The premium's level depends on the numerical method.** The paper's
numbers come from a 30-point grid, and on that grid the simulation
prints a value premium of 5.3.
[Chapter 7](07-quadrature-solution.qmd) refines the grid until the
solution stops moving, and the converged premium is near 3.5. The
mechanism survives, because at every grid size the spread is positive
and ordered by the measured leverages. Roughly a third of the headline
level, though, is numerical approximation rather than economics. Quote
the mechanism with confidence, and quote the level with a footnote
about the grid size.

**The risk-free rate is too high.** The model prints a mean risk-free
rate of 1.58 percent against 0.91 in the data. With an elasticity of
intertemporal substitution above one, the rate stays low and stable
enough to be plausible, which is why the calibration insists on
$\psi = 1.5$. Two-thirds of a point is still a miss. The level of every
expected return in the model inherits a small upward bias from it, even
where the spreads between claims are right.

The pattern across the four misses is consistent. The model is at its
best on orderings and spreads driven by measured cash-flow exposures,
and it is at its weakest on levels and comovements. Trust its rankings
more than its levels.

## Takeaways

- The five standing objections have answers, and each answer is a
  measurement, not a rhetorical move, e.g., preferences are the minimal
  separation ([Chapter 4](04-epstein-zin-preferences.qmd)), the
  loadings are in the dividend data
  ([Chapter 8](08-calibrating-cash-flows.qmd)), and any claim can be
  priced by the same steps
  ([Chapter 11](11-price-your-own-claim.qmd)).
- The model's reliable outputs are cross-sectional: which claim earns
  more, ordered by measured leverage, and roughly by how much relative
  to the others.
- Its unreliable outputs are levels and comovements: return
  correlations too low (0.44 model, 0.75 data), value's dividend
  persistence too high (0.29 against 0.06), a premium level that moves
  from 5.3 to roughly 3.5 under grid refinement, and a risk-free rate
  of 1.58 against 0.91.
- The course proves existence only. The value premium can be
  compensation for long-run consumption risk in one disciplined
  economy. The claim is strong, and it is the only claim the course
  makes.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Recall"}
Answer from memory before opening.

1. What kind of answers does the chapter give to the standing
   objections: rhetorical or something else?
2. Where does the chapter say the model is genuinely vulnerable, and
   what should you accordingly trust?

**Answers.**

1. Measurements, each one a computation rather than a rhetorical move.
2. The magnitude depends on the method (finer grids print smaller
   premia) and short samples leave the loadings imprecise. Trust the
   ordering and the channel; treat exact levels as uncertain.
:::
